items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-24
items.q: I don't, I can't, I can't find it in me to tar Whiteman with the same brush. I always heard it in Biggs' playing, except in the Wolverine days.

ctx.x: Wouldn't the Whiteman Orchestra be a better representation of your kind of, your image of that foggy romanticism? And Biggs' playing within the Whiteman Orchestra was an antidote to that kind of saccharine?

That's a very good point. And I suppose there are degrees of that too. It may be that Biggs' presentation was more sophisticated than Whiteman's. But I still see it as part of the same package. Not only Biggs with Whiteman, but also Biggs with Goldkett or Biggs with Trumbauer. I don't, I can't, I can't find it in me to tar Whiteman with the same brush. I always heard it in Biggs' playing, except in the Wolverine days.

To my mind, the best of jazz or, if you want to call that music that he's playing jazz, which I think it was to a certain extent. I mean, you know, even within the New Orleans context. The best of it is, to my mind, is it has a very unsentimental quality to it. That is good jazz, it's not sentimental, it's not gimmicky, it doesn't have, it doesn't play cheap tricks on the emotions and things like that. Biggs' music, to me, does none of those things. It does not play cheap tricks on the emotions, but... I believe…
